analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care after childbirth.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote or a single cosponsor and died in a House subcommittee when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any health plan that covers maternity care to pay for at least 48 hours of inpatient hospital care after a vaginal delivery and 120 hours after a cesarean section, unless a doctor approved an earlier discharge. It also would have required coverage of a nurse or home visit within 24 hours for mothers who leave early, plus parenting classes such as feeding training, and it set civil fines for insurers that failed to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Mothers and newborns on private health insurance, who in the mid-1990s were often discharged from the hospital within a day or even hours of delivery. The bill would have guaranteed them a minimum hospital stay, an early home visit if they left sooner, feeding instruction, and medical checkups, all covered by their plan without extra charge. Obstetricians, pediatricians, and hospitals also benefit because insurers could not penalize doctors for ordering care consistent with the law, and hospitals would be reimbursed for longer stays.

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees coverage for at least 48 hours of hospital care after a vaginal delivery and 120 hours after a cesarean section, ending the practice of insurers pushing mothers and infants out of the hospital within hours of birth [S2][S3].

If a mother chooses to leave early, the plan must cover one home visit within 24 hours of discharge, plus parental education including breast- or bottle-feeding training and clinical assessments of mother and baby [S2][S3].

Doctors are protected: the Health and Human Services Secretary must write rules so plans cannot penalize a practitioner for providing care consistent with the mandate, and violators face civil money penalties [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and, through premiums, the employers and policyholders who fund coverage. Longer hospital stays and home visits cost money, and the mandate applies to every plan that offers maternity benefits, so the cost would flow into premiums and employer benefit budgets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and their premium payers

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises coverage costs for every maternity-bearing plan, and those costs ultimately show up in premiums paid by employers and enrollees, including people who never give birth [S3].

A fixed 48/120-hour floor is one-size-fits-all: some healthy mothers and babies do fine leaving early with a home visit, and some need far more than two days, so a rigid minimum neither saves the most money nor helps the neediest cases the most [S3].

The bill covered only plans that offer maternity benefits and relied on regulations and fines for enforcement, so plans had room to comply minimally, and early-discharge patients who opted out before 48 hours got only a single home visit [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to mothers and newborns was significant and immediate: newborns and mothers recovering from childbirth, especially cesarean patients, get time for feeding to be established and complications to surface, with a home visit as a safety net. The cost is real but spread thin across all premium payers, which is why minimum-stay mandates of this kind became one of the most widely adopted insurance reforms of the era. The main design weakness is the rigid hour count rather than a standard based on medical readiness, but the bill let any mother leave early voluntarily with a covered home visit, which blunts the sharpest objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, where it sat until the two-year Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a vote, or even a cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Edolphus Towns introduced the Mother and Child Protection Act of 1996 on March 14, 1996, requiring health plans to cover at least 48 hours of post-delivery hospital care for vaginal births and 120 hours for cesareans [S1][S3][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and, two weeks later, on March 29, 1996, was passed down to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment [S5].
No cosponsors ever joined [S4], and no further action was taken before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the bill expired in subcommittee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the employers who buy coverage for their workers are better off because the bill never advanced, since they avoided a new mandate to pay for longer post-delivery hospital stays. Insured mothers and newborns got no federal guarantee of a minimum hospital stay from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor, but recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership (Chair Thomas Bliley)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over health insurance bills
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment and never scheduled a markup or floor action on it during the remaining months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill forced any plan offering maternity benefits to pay for 48-120 hour hospital stays, home visits, and parental education, with civil fines for noncompliance. Insurers and employers paying premiums would have borne that added cost, which is the core of the bill's transfer from industry to patients.

Longer guaranteed stays and mandatory home visits mean more reimbursed days and services after every delivery, and the bill barred plans from penalizing doctors who followed it. New mothers and newborns benefit through the same longer stays, so the industry's interest runs alongside patients' here.
